paragraphs: Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.
### Apple working on AI agent that can code, browse the web, more

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.
Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.
The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Last month, Apple announced plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access, with changes introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta that give users more granular control over which apps and information third-party AI agents can access.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.
Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.
One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.
With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.
To read Bloomberg’s report, follow this link.

paragraphs: OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

Today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.
### What’s new in GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol?
Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.
On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.
“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI says.
Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.
Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.
With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

“Some of you have been asking very politely. Some of you have just been asking. GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available. Super efficient and built to perform where it counts—the real world.” — OpenAI (@OpenAI)
### Who gets GPT-6.2?
Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu.

The $200/month Pro plan also gets Ultrafast mode for the first time with Sol. The $500/month Pro plan gets Ultrafast on both models, as do eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces once an admin enables it.
How fast is Ultrafast? OpenAI says it can generate tokens at up to 4.5 times the standard rate on either model, although it uses more of your allowance. You can switch speeds from the model picker.
Developers can use both models through the API today as well. Astra’s standard input and output prices are 20% lower than with GPT-6 Astra, while Sol keeps its GPT-6.1 pricing.
You can read more in OpenAI’s full announcement.

https://9to5mac.com/2026/07/01/safaris-n.summary: Apple is introducing a new MCP server for Safari that lets coding agents inspect websites directly in the browser. Here are the details.
https://9to5mac.com/2026/07/01/safaris-n.author: Marcus Mendes
https://9to5mac.com/2026/07/01/safaris-n.lead_paragraph: Apple is introducing a new MCP server for Safari that lets coding agents inspect websites directly in the browser, giving them access to page content, console logs, network requests, screenshots, and more. Here are the details.
paragraphs: Apple is introducing a new MCP server for Safari that lets coding agents inspect websites directly in the browser, giving them access to page content, console logs, network requests, screenshots, and more. Here are the details.
### MCP server included in Safari Technology Preview 247

In a new post published on the WebKit blog, Apple says that Safari Technology Preview 247 includes the Safari MCP server, “a Model Context Protocol server for web developers that makes your web development and debugging workflow faster and more powerful.”

We know agents are increasingly integral to the coding process and the Safari MCP server gives your agent the ability to know how your code actually renders in the browser by connecting it to a Safari browser window.

MCP is an open standard created by Anthropic and later donated to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation. It essentially provides a common way for compatible AI agents to connect to external tools, services, and data sources, allowing them to retrieve information and perform authorized actions rather than relying solely on what users paste into a chat.

In practice, MCP can allow compatible clients such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to connect to MCP servers that expose services and resources, including GitHub, Slack, Google Drive, Notion, databases, local files, and browser-development tools.

With the new server configured in Safari Technology Preview 247, coding agents can inspect webpages, access console logs and network requests, capture screenshots, and interact with elements on the page.
Here’s a use case described in Apple’s post:

You see something wrong with your site in the browser. You open the console to hunt it down. You click into the styles tab. You see what’s broken. You go back to your code to fix it. Or maybe you take a screenshot, detail the problem to your agent, and let it do the fixing for you. Hopefully it gets it right, the bug is fixed, and you can move on. But when it isn’t fixed, you go through the workflow again — Browser. Prompt. Agent. And again and again, until you finally squash the bug. Regardless of the browser or tools you use, the debugging workflow is a lot of clicks, tools, and window hopping to make a single fix, but it doesn’t have to be that way. If you’re already using agents in your development workflow, the Safari MCP server makes your debugging faster and more efficient.

The post outlines several potential uses for the Safari MCP server, including helping agents debug websites, identify Safari compatibility issues, analyze performance, check accessibility, and verify various page and user-interface states.

Additionally, the post lists and describes nearly 20 tools included in the server, such as browser_console_messages to “return buffered console logs for the current or specified tab,” screenshot to “capture a screenshot of the current page as a PNG,” list_network_requests to “list network request summaries (URL, method, status, timing) for the current tab,” and page_interactions to “perform DOM interactions in sequence: click, type, scroll, hover, keyPress, etc.”
To learn how to get started and make use of MCP on safari with Claude, Codex, and more, follow this link.
